catalog_quote: [Chafe 1967:3, sec. 1.1] Every complete word contains at the most only one strong stress that is morphologically conditioned, although syntactic factors may add another stress when the word occurs in a complete utterance. A vowel is morphologically stressed if it is even, prefinal, and basically strong. If the prefinal vowel of a word is odd or basically weak, stress will occur on the nearest preceding even vowel that is either basically strong itself or has somewhere between it and any even prefinal vowel, if there is one, either (a) a basically strong vowel, (b) h or ?, (c) a cluster of two consonants not including n, w, or y, or (d) sn, sw, or ... sy. Many words have no morphological strong stress. Vowel length is in a sense complementary to stress ... sweep_summary: Seneca (sene1264, in catalog as weight-hedged, deciding source Chafe 1967). Three works with stress in the title, all about Seneca word accent. (1) Melinger 2002 (IJAL 68) was already held by the project (MPG PuRe open copy) and was read: rule (2) p.290 restates the closure-conditioned even-syllable rule and, citing Chafe 1996/1998, reports multiple equal-pitch accents per word and pitch as the sole correlate -- this refines the catalog's 'at most one strong stress' deciding quote without displacing Chafe 1967 as primary (the rule is 'adapted from Chafe 1996'; the better first-hand update would be Chafe 1996 HNAI sketch or Chafe 2015 grammar, neither in this search of works with stress in the title's items). (2) Michelson 1983 Harvard dissertation (published 1988 as A Comparative Study of Lake-Iroquoian Accent, Kluwer): only bibliographic records reached -- Springer DOI paywalled, archive.org copy lending-only, HathiTrust search-only; not read, priority medium. (3) Chafe 1977 (SCOPIL 4, pp.169-181): no digital copy found on archive.org, HathiTrust, Google Books or Crossref; print-only; the catalog already carries its p.178 Seneca passage second-hand via StressTyp2; priority medium for first-hand verification.org advancedsearch/metadata/MARC, HathiTrust bib API, Crossref, Open Library, Google Books); Springer, HathiTrust catalog and WorldCat search pages returned bot challenges/429.

new_statements.reading: Confirms the catalog's placement coding (closure-conditioned weight, even-syllable count from the left, unbounded, accentless words possible) and refines its count claim: the deciding Chafe 1967 quote says a word has at most one strong stress, whereas Melinger, following Chafe 1996/1998, reports that every qualifying even syllable is accented with equal high pitch, and that the accent is pitch-only ('nonstress accent'). Melinger's rule is a secondary restatement explicitly adapted from Chafe 1996, so it does not displace the primary.

audit.recode_to: Keep classification weight-hedged (quantity-sensitive by closure: CVC heavy where coda = obstruent before obstruent/laryngeal, intervocalic h/?, or s before n/w; even-numbered non-final syllables counted from the left) — Melinger 2002 p.289-290 confirms this. reclassify the secondary-stress / culminativity fields: the secondary-stress rule from 'none at word level (no word has more than one strong stress, Chafe 1967:11)' to 'every qualifying even-numbered non-final syllable is accented with equally high pitch; words may carry several accents with no primary/secondary hierarchy, or none (Chafe 1996; 1998 apud Melinger 2002:291-292)'; edge/the primary-stress rule should no longer say strong stress falls only on the rightmost qualifying even vowel; add a caution that the correlate is pitch only (nonstress accent, Melinger 2002:288) and that even penults lengthened by EPL are not accented. Verify final wording against Chafe 2015 before shipping.
